claim: The cortical network can be hierarchically ordered based on the anatomy of interareal cortico-cortical (CC) projections.
source: The complex network of cortical areas can be hierarchically ordered based on the anatomy of interareal cortico-cortical (CC) projections.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on cortical hierarchy.

claim: Lower cortical areas send bottom-up 'feedforward' (FF) inputs to higher areas.
source: Lower areas send bottom-up 'feedforward' (FF) inputs to higher areas, which reciprocate with anatomically distinct top-down 'feedback' (FB) inputs, while areas at the same hierarchical level interact through 'lateral' or 'mixed' inputs (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Markov et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Felleman and Van Essen, 1991 and Markov et al., 2013.

claim: Higher cortical areas reciprocate with anatomically distinct top-down 'feedback' (FB) inputs.
source: Lower areas send bottom-up 'feedforward' (FF) inputs to higher areas, which reciprocate with anatomically distinct top-down 'feedback' (FB) inputs, while areas at the same hierarchical level interact through 'lateral' or 'mixed' inputs (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Markov et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Felleman and Van Essen, 1991 and Markov et al., 2013.

claim: Areas at the same hierarchical level interact through 'lateral' or 'mixed' inputs.
source: Lower areas send bottom-up 'feedforward' (FF) inputs to higher areas, which reciprocate with anatomically distinct top-down 'feedback' (FB) inputs, while areas at the same hierarchical level interact through 'lateral' or 'mixed' inputs (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Markov et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Felleman and Van Essen, 1991 and Markov et al., 2013.

claim: A similar hierarchical architecture is observed across cortical areas and across species.
source: The fact that a similar hierarchical architecture is observed across areas and across species (D'Souza et al., 2020; Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Harris et al., 2019) suggests that FF and FB interactions reside at the core of cortical function.
evidence: This is supported by citations to D'Souza et al., 2020, Felleman and Van Essen, 1991, and Harris et al., 2019.

claim: FF and FB interactions reside at the core of cortical function.
source: The fact that a similar hierarchical architecture is observed across areas and across species (D'Souza et al., 2020; Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Harris et al., 2019) suggests that FF and FB interactions reside at the core of cortical function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of conserved hierarchical architecture across areas and species.

claim: Local cortical circuits are posited to implement a conserved canonical computation in different cortical areas.
source: As with local cortical circuits, posited to implement a conserved canonical computation in different cortical areas (Douglas and Martin, 2004; Harris and Shepherd, 2015), long-range cortical connections could be performing stereotyped functions in different areas and in different species.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Douglas and Martin, 2004 and Harris and Shepherd, 2015.

claim: Long-range cortical connections could be performing stereotyped functions in different areas and in different species.
source: As with local cortical circuits, posited to implement a conserved canonical computation in different cortical areas (Douglas and Martin, 2004; Harris and Shepherd, 2015), long-range cortical connections could be performing stereotyped functions in different areas and in different species.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential function of long-range cortical connections.

claim: The precise function of FF and FB interactions in hierarchical processing remains poorly understood.
source: However, the precise function of FF and FB interactions in hierarchical processing remains poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Several theories of hierarchical computation involve looped interactions between areas.
source: Several theories of hierarchical computation involve looped interactions between areas, in which FF and FB pathways selectively influence each other in a bidirectional manner (Bastos et al., 2012; Guerguiev et al., 2017; Keller and Mrsic-Flogel, 2018; Lillicrap et al., 2016; Rao and Ballard, 1999; Roelfsema and Holtmaat, 2018; Sacramento et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to theoretical work.

claim: In looped interaction theories, FF and FB pathways selectively influence each other in a bidirectional manner.
source: Several theories of hierarchical computation involve looped interactions between areas, in which FF and FB pathways selectively influence each other in a bidirectional manner (Bastos et al., 2012; Guerguiev et al., 2017; Keller and Mrsic-Flogel, 2018; Lillicrap et al., 2016; Rao and Ballard, 1999; Roelfsema and Holtmaat, 2018; Sacramento et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to theoretical work.

claim: Cortical areas are densely interconnected.
source: It is well established that cortical areas are densely interconnected and that FF pathways are always reciprocated by FB projections (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Gămănuţ et al., 2018; Oh et al., 2014; Zingg et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: FF pathways are always reciprocated by FB projections.
source: It is well established that cortical areas are densely interconnected and that FF pathways are always reciprocated by FB projections (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Gămănuţ et al., 2018; Oh et al., 2014; Zingg et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Whether CC connections are wired to selectively facilitate looped computations remains unknown.
source: However, whether CC connections are wired to selectively facilitate looped computations remains unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: CC inputs could modulate neurons projecting back to the source of those inputs indirectly via intermediary inhibitory or excitatory cells.
source: One possibility is that CC inputs specifically modulate neurons projecting back to the source of those inputs (looped neurons) indirectly via intermediary inhibitory or excitatory cells in the local circuit.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible mechanism.

claim: CC projections could selectively synapse onto looped neurons directly to form interareal monosynaptic loops.
source: Another possibility, not mutually exclusive to the previous one, is that CC projections selectively synapse onto looped neurons directly to form interareal monosynaptic loops, which would be excitatory since most long-range cortical afferents are glutamatergic.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible mechanism, with supporting knowledge about glutamatergic afferents.

claim: Most long-range cortical afferents are glutamatergic.
source: Another possibility, not mutually exclusive to the previous one, is that CC projections selectively synapse onto looped neurons directly to form interareal monosynaptic loops, which would be excitatory since most long-range cortical afferents are glutamatergic.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cortical afferents.

claim: Cortical projection neurons can be divided into three broad classes: intratelencephalic (IT) neurons, pyramidal tract (PT) neurons, and corticothalamic (CT) neurons.
source: Cortical projection neurons can be divided into three broad classes: intratelencephalic (IT) neurons, which project to cortical areas, pyramidal tract (PT) neurons, which project to multiple subcerebral areas including the midbrain, and corticothalamic (CT) neurons, which project predominantly to the thalamus (Gerfen et al., 2018; Harris and Shepherd, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gerfen et al., 2018 and Harris and Shepherd, 2015.

claim: IT neurons project to cortical areas.
source: Cortical projection neurons can be divided into three broad classes: intratelencephalic (IT) neurons, which project to cortical areas, pyramidal tract (PT) neurons, which project to multiple subcerebral areas including the midbrain, and corticothalamic (CT) neurons, which project predominantly to the thalamus (Gerfen et al., 2018; Harris and Shepherd, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gerfen et al., 2018 and Harris and Shepherd, 2015.

claim: PT neurons project to multiple subcerebral areas including the midbrain.
source: Cortical projection neurons can be divided into three broad classes: intratelencephalic (IT) neurons, which project to cortical areas, pyramidal tract (PT) neurons, which project to multiple subcerebral areas including the midbrain, and corticothalamic (CT) neurons, which project predominantly to the thalamus (Gerfen et al., 2018; Harris and Shepherd, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gerfen et al., 2018 and Harris and Shepherd, 2015.

claim: CT neurons project predominantly to the thalamus.
source: Cortical projection neurons can be divided into three broad classes: intratelencephalic (IT) neurons, which project to cortical areas, pyramidal tract (PT) neurons, which project to multiple subcerebral areas including the midbrain, and corticothalamic (CT) neurons, which project predominantly to the thalamus (Gerfen et al., 2018; Harris and Shepherd, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gerfen et al., 2018 and Harris and Shepherd, 2015.

claim: Previous studies have found that CC inputs form monosynaptic loops in sensorimotor cortices.
source: Previous studies have found that CC inputs form monosynaptic loops in sensorimotor (Kinnischtzke et al., 2016; Mao et al., 2011; Yamawaki et al., 2016), frontal (Zhang et al., 2016), and visual cortices (Johnson and Burkhalter, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kinnischtzke et al., 2016, Mao et al., 2011, and Yamawaki et al., 2016.

claim: Previous studies have found that CC inputs form monosynaptic loops in frontal cortices.
source: Previous studies have found that CC inputs form monosynaptic loops in sensorimotor (Kinnischtzke et al., 2016; Mao et al., 2011; Yamawaki et al., 2016), frontal (Zhang et al., 2016), and visual cortices (Johnson and Burkhalter, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2016.

claim: Previous studies have found that CC inputs form monosynaptic loops in visual cortices.
source: Previous studies have found that CC inputs form monosynaptic loops in sensorimotor (Kinnischtzke et al., 2016; Mao et al., 2011; Yamawaki et al., 2016), frontal (Zhang et al., 2016), and visual cortices (Johnson and Burkhalter, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Johnson and Burkhalter, 1997.

claim: There is evidence that some CC projections selectively innervate IT neurons over PT and CT neurons.
source: There is also evidence that some CC projections selectively innervate IT neurons over PT and CT neurons (Kim et al., 2015; Kinnischtzke et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016), but also evidence that some do not (Yamawaki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2015, Kinnischtzke et al., 2016, and Zhang et al., 2016.

claim: There is evidence that some CC projections do not selectively innervate IT neurons over PT and CT neurons.
source: There is also evidence that some CC projections selectively innervate IT neurons over PT and CT neurons (Kim et al., 2015; Kinnischtzke et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016), but also evidence that some do not (Yamawaki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yamawaki et al., 2016.

claim: It remains unknown whether CC inputs selectively contact looped neurons over closely intermingled IT neurons projecting elsewhere.
source: However, it remains unknown whether CC inputs selectively contact looped neurons over closely intermingled IT neurons projecting elsewhere (non-looped IT neurons), or whether they innervate IT neurons equally regardless of their projection pattern.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: It remains unknown whether the selectivity of CC input between two areas is similar for both ascending and descending projections.
source: Furthermore, in order to implement selective recurrent interactions, both FF and FB connections could be required to specifically engage with looped IT neurons. Yet, whether the selectivity of CC input between two areas is similar for both ascending and descending projections or whether it varies also remains unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: FF and FB axons selectively provide stronger inputs to looped neurons in layer (L) 5 and L6.
source: Using a combination of subcellular channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2)-assisted circuit mapping (sCRACM) (Petreanu et al., 2009) and injections of multiple retrograde tracers, we found that FF and FB axons selectively provide stronger inputs to looped neurons in layer (L) 5 and L6, while in L2/3, they remain either unselective for projection type or provide stronger inputs to non-looped neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: In L2/3, FF and FB axons remain either unselective for projection type or provide stronger inputs to non-looped neurons.
source: Using a combination of subcellular channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2)-assisted circuit mapping (sCRACM) (Petreanu et al., 2009) and injections of multiple retrograde tracers, we found that FF and FB axons selectively provide stronger inputs to looped neurons in layer (L) 5 and L6, while in L2/3, they remain either unselective for projection type or provide stronger inputs to non-looped neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Both ascending and descending hierarchical streams display the same selectivity for specific looped projection neurons despite their different anatomical profiles.
source: Thus, both ascending and descending hierarchical streams display the same selectivity for specific looped projection neurons despite their different anatomical profiles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Preferential innervation of looped L5 neurons often involved synapses made on their apical, but not basal, dendrites.
source: Moreover, preferential innervation of looped L5 neurons often involved synapses made on their apical, but not basal, dendrites.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Neurons with different projection patterns are intermingled in V1 and V2L.
source: In each case, the different projection neurons were closely intermingled (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: In both V1 and V2L, IT neurons were distributed across all layers except L1, including L4.
source: In both V1 and V2L, IT neurons were distributed across all layers except L1, including L4 (Harris et al., 2019; Minamisawa et al., 2018), indicating that FF and FB projections originate from neurons spanning most of the cortical depth.
evidence: This is supported by data and citations to Harris et al., 2019 and Minamisawa et al., 2018.

claim: FF and FB projections originate from neurons spanning most of the cortical depth.
source: In both V1 and V2L, IT neurons were distributed across all layers except L1, including L4 (Harris et al., 2019; Minamisawa et al., 2018), indicating that FF and FB projections originate from neurons spanning most of the cortical depth.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the distribution of IT neurons.

claim: PT and CT neurons were confined to L5 and L5/6, respectively.
source: In contrast, PT and CT neurons were confined to L5 and L5/6, respectively, as previously described (Harris and Shepherd, 2015; Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A,B and citation to Harris and Shepherd, 2015.

claim: Double-labeled IT neurons were found in L2–6 after injecting tracers in two different cortical areas.
source: In both V1 and V2L, we found double-labeled IT neurons in L2–6 after injecting tracers in two different cortical areas, indicating that subpopulations of ascending and descending projection neurons have diverging axons innervating more than one visual cortical area (Han et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to Han et al., 2018.

claim: Subpopulations of ascending and descending projection neurons have diverging axons innervating more than one visual cortical area.
source: In both V1 and V2L, we found double-labeled IT neurons in L2–6 after injecting tracers in two different cortical areas, indicating that subpopulations of ascending and descending projection neurons have diverging axons innervating more than one visual cortical area (Han et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of double-labeled IT neurons, supported by citation to Han et al., 2018.

claim: IT neurons were rarely double-labeled when tracers were injected in a cortical and subcortical area.
source: However, IT neurons were rarely double-labeled when tracers were injected in a cortical and subcortical area, confirming that cortical- and subcortical-projecting neurons constitute different classes of projection neurons (Economo et al., 2018; Harris and Shepherd, 2015; Tasic et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to Economo et al., 2018, Harris and Shepherd, 2015, and Tasic et al., 2018.

claim: Cortical- and subcortical-projecting neurons constitute different classes of projection neurons.
source: However, IT neurons were rarely double-labeled when tracers were injected in a cortical and subcortical area, confirming that cortical- and subcortical-projecting neurons constitute different classes of projection neurons (Economo et al., 2018; Harris and Shepherd, 2015; Tasic et al., 2018).
evidence: This is confirmed by experimental data and citations to Economo et al., 2018, Harris and Shepherd, 2015, and Tasic et al., 2018.

claim: FF axons in V2L were present in all layers but were denser in L2/3 and L6.
source: FF axons in V2L were present in all layers but were denser in L2/3 and L6.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: FB axons in V1 arborized in L1 and L6, while avoiding middle layers.
source: FB axons in V1 arborized in L1 and L6, while avoiding middle layers.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: FF and FB projections could potentially directly innervate both looped and non-looped IT neurons in each cortical layer, as well as PT and CT neurons in L5 and L6.
source: Given the laminar distribution of the different projection neurons and the termination pattern of CC afferent axons, FF and FB projections could potentially directly innervate both looped and non-looped IT neurons in each cortical layer, as well as PT and CT neurons in L5 and L6 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the laminar distribution data and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The proximity of looped IT neurons and other projection classes indicates that FF and FB axons are equally accessible to them.
source: Moreover, the proximity of looped IT neurons and other projection classes indicates that FF and FB axons are equally accessible to them.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of intermingled neurons.

claim: Axo-dendritic overlap does not always predict connectivity.
source: Thus, functional mapping of FF and FB connections is required to reveal any underlying synaptic specificity, since axo-dendritic overlap does not always predict connectivity (Harris and Shepherd, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Harris and Shepherd, 2015.

claim: The onset of laser-evoked EPSCs was delayed relative to laser pulse onset in 96% (225/235) of the recorded neurons labeled with retrograde tracers.
source: The onset of laser-evoked EPSCs was delayed relative to laser pulse onset in 96% (225/235) of the recorded neurons labeled with retrograde tracers, indicating that retrograde AAV-mediated transfection of ChR2 was rare, consistent with histological analyses (Materials and methods, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and histological analyses shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Retrograde AAV-mediated transfection of ChR2 was rare.
source: The onset of laser-evoked EPSCs was delayed relative to laser pulse onset in 96% (225/235) of the recorded neurons labeled with retrograde tracers, indicating that retrograde AAV-mediated transfection of ChR2 was rare, consistent with histological analyses (Materials and methods, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the delayed onset of EPSCs and supported by histological analyses.

claim: sCRACM maps provide a measure of both the strength and location of monosynaptic CC inputs with minimal contamination from local collaterals.
source: Thus, sCRACM maps provide a measure of both the strength and location of monosynaptic CC inputs with minimal contamination from local collaterals.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the low rate of retrograde transfection.

claim: FF inputs were largely confined to perisomatic dendrites in L2/3.
source: In L2/3, FF inputs were largely confined to perisomatic dendrites.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In L6, FF connections targeted perisomatic dendrites in both CT and IT neurons.
source: In L6, while FF connections also targeted perisomatic dendrites in both CT and IT neurons, we could detect additional FF input on the apical dendrites of IT neurons extending across L5 (Figure 3A, Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 4F.

claim: Additional FF input was detected on the apical dendrites of L6 IT neurons extending across L5.
source: In L6, while FF connections also targeted perisomatic dendrites in both CT and IT neurons, we could detect additional FF input on the apical dendrites of IT neurons extending across L5 (Figure 3A, Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 4F.

claim: FF input contacted L5 IT neurons in both the perisomatic dendrites and along their apical dendritic trunk spanning L4 and L2/3.
source: Similarly, FF input contacted L5 IT neurons in both the perisomatic dendrites and along their apical dendritic trunk spanning L4 and L2/3 (Figure 3A, Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 5B.

claim: FF axons innervate several dendritic domains of L5 pyramidal neurons.
source: Thus, like other long-range inputs (Petreanu et al., 2009), FF axons innervate several dendritic domains of L5 pyramidal neurons, revealing that targeting of apical dendrites is not an exclusive property of FB axons (see below).
evidence: This is supported by data and citation to Petreanu et al., 2009.

claim: Targeting of apical dendrites is not an exclusive property of FB axons.
source: Thus, like other long-range inputs (Petreanu et al., 2009), FF axons innervate several dendritic domains of L5 pyramidal neurons, revealing that targeting of apical dendrites is not an exclusive property of FB axons (see below).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that FF axons also target apical dendrites.

claim: FB afferents innervated the perisomatic compartments of all recorded cell types.
source: As with FF inputs, FB afferents innervated the perisomatic compartments of all recorded cell types.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A larger fraction of FB to L2/3 and L5 neurons was located on their distal dendrites in L1 compared to FF inputs.
source: However, when compared to FF inputs, a larger fraction of FB to L2/3 and L5 neurons was located on their distal dendrites in L1 (Figure 3B), consistent with previous measurements (Petreanu et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2013) and with the laminar profile of FB axons (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 1C, and citations to Petreanu et al., 2009 and Yang et al., 2013.

claim: Apical tuft inputs were more readily detected in L5 IT neurons than in PT neurons.
source: Apical tuft inputs were more readily detected in L5 IT neurons than in PT neurons, suggesting differential innervation by FB fibers (Figure 2G, Figure 3B and Figure 5N, see below).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2G, Figure 3B, and Figure 5N.

claim: For V1→V2L inputs, total strength was greater in looped IT neurons than in non-looped IT neurons in L6.
source: For V1→V2L inputs, total strength was greater in looped IT neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; SRI: −0.49 ± 0.23, p=0.002).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: For V1→V2L inputs, stronger innervation of looped IT neurons was present in both perisomatic and apical areas in L6.
source: This stronger innervation was present in both perisomatic (SRI: −0.50 ± 0.21, p=0.0001) and apical areas (SRI: −0.45 ± 0.45, p=0.0364) (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A–D.

claim: For V1→V2M inputs, looped IT neurons received significantly stronger input in the perisomatic area in L6.
source: For V1→V2M inputs, we did not detect a difference in total strength between looped and non-looped IT neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, SRI: −0.32 ± 0.48, p=0.064), but looped IT neurons again received significantly stronger input in the perisomatic area (Figure 4C; SRI: −0.36 ± 0.46, p=0.038).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: V1→V2M inputs in apical dendrites of L6 neurons were mostly weak and not different between looped and non-looped cell types.
source: V1→V2M inputs in apical dendrites were mostly weak and not different between cell types (Apical SRI: 0.33 ± 0.69, p=0.247).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Total V1 FF input to looped L6 IT neurons was consistently stronger than to CT neurons in V2L.
source: We next compared V1 FF inputs to looped L6 IT neurons and same-layer CT neurons in V2L. Total input to looped neurons was consistently stronger than to CT neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, SRI: −0.64 ± 0.23, p=1.2×10−5) and inputs were weaker in both perisomatic and apical areas of CT neurons (Figure 4E–H, Perisomatic SRI: −0.64 ± 0.26, p=2.4×10−5; Apical SRI: −0.69 ± 0.40, p=0.018).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E–H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: V1 FF inputs were weaker in both perisomatic and apical areas of L6 CT neurons compared to looped IT neurons in V2L.
source: We next compared V1 FF inputs to looped L6 IT neurons and same-layer CT neurons in V2L. Total input to looped neurons was consistently stronger than to CT neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, SRI: −0.64 ± 0.23, p=1.2×10−5) and inputs were weaker in both perisomatic and apical areas of CT neurons (Figure 4E–H, Perisomatic SRI: −0.64 ± 0.26, p=2.4×10−5; Apical SRI: −0.69 ± 0.40, p=0.018).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E–H.

claim: FB from V2M preferentially connected to L6 IT neurons projecting back to the source of FB, both when measuring total and perisomatic input.
source: For the looped vs. non-looped comparison among IT neurons, FB from V2M preferentially connected to IT neurons projecting back to the source of FB, both when measuring total and perisomatic input (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4I–L, Total SRI: −0.39 ± 0.36, p=0.031; Perisomatic SRI: −0.40 ± 0.36, p=0.028), but no difference was detected in the apical area (SRI: −0.27 ± 0.85, p=0.56).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4I–L and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: FB from V2L was not significantly different in looped and non-looped L6 IT neurons.
source: FB from V2L was not significantly different in looped and non-looped L6 IT neurons (total SRI: −0.18 ± 0.35, p=0.098; perisomatic SRI: −0.14 ± 0.35, p=0.182; apical SRI: −0.02 ± 0.90, p=0.958).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Looped L6 neurons received stronger perisomatic input from V2L compared to neighboring CT neurons.
source: However, looped neurons received stronger perisomatic input from V2L compared to neighboring CT neurons (Figure 4M–P; total SRI: −0.40 ± 0.42, p=0.003, perisomatic SRI: −0.41 ± 0.45, p=0.005).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4M–P.

claim: In most experiments (three out of four), FF and FB connections to L6 neurons were significantly stronger in looped IT cells than in non-looped ones.
source: Thus, we found that in most experiments (three out of four), FF and FB connections to L6 neurons were significantly stronger in looped IT cells than in non-looped ones.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: FF and FB connections were stronger in looped L6 IT neurons than in CT neurons.
source: FF and FB connections were also stronger in looped IT neurons than in CT neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: In V2L, total input strength did not differ between looped and non-looped L5 IT neurons for V1 FF inputs.
source: In V2L, total input strength did not differ between looped and non-looped L5 IT neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; SRI: −0.03 ± 0.35, p=0.783), and neither did perisomatic input (Figure 5C; SRI: −0.02 ± 0.36, p=0.82).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: V1 FF inputs terminating on the apical dendrites of L5 neurons in V2L were stronger in looped IT neurons.
source: However, FF inputs terminating on the apical dendrites of L5 neurons were stronger in looped IT neurons (Figure 5D; SRI: −0.40 ± 0.43, p=0.009).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In V2M, looped L5 neurons received stronger V1 input than neighboring non-looped IT neurons on both their perisomatic and apical dendrites.
source: In V2M, looped neurons received stronger V1 input than neighboring non-looped IT neurons on both their perisomatic and apical dendrites (Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5C,D; total SRI: −0.42 ± 0.32, p=0.002; perisomatic SRI: −0.42 ± 0.35, p=0.002; apical SRI: −0.37 ± 0.43, p=0.0174).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C,D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: FF fibers innervated the perisomatic dendrites of looped L5 IT neurons more strongly than PT neurons, with no difference observed in apical inputs.
source: We then compared the strength of FF inputs to looped IT and PT neurons. FF fibers innervated the perisomatic dendrites of looped neurons more strongly, with no difference observed in apical inputs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5E–H; total SRI: −0.43 ± 0.41, p=0.003; perisomatic SRI: −0.46 ± 0.43, p=0.002; apical SRI: −0.14 ± 0.65, p=0.49).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5E–H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: FF inputs are selectively stronger in looped L5 neurons when compared to non-looped IT or PT neurons.
source: We conclude that FF inputs are selectively stronger in looped L5 neurons when compared to non-looped IT or PT neurons, and that this selectivity may result from inputs impinging on the perisomatic dendrites (V1→V2L, IT vs. PT), the apical dendrites (V1→V2L, IT vs. IT), or both regions (V1→V2M, IT vs. IT).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: For V2L→V1 and V2M→V1 FB inputs, total input and perisomatic input were indistinguishable between looped and non-looped L5 IT neurons.
source: We first compared the strength of V2L→V1 and V2M→V1 FB inputs to looped vs. non-looped L5 IT neurons (Figure 5I–L). In both projections, total input (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; V2L→V1 SRI: −0.15 ± 0.54, p=0.284; V2M→V1 SRI: −0.19 ± 0.56, p=0.222) and perisomatic input (Figure 5K; V2L→V1 SRI: −0.09 ± 0.60, p=0.557; V2M→V1 SRI: −0.22 ± 0.57, p=0.152) were indistinguishable between the two projection types.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5I–L, Figure 5K, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: FB inputs targeting the distal tufts in L1 were stronger in looped than non-looped L5 IT neurons for both V2L→V1 and V2M→V1 projections.
source: However, inputs targeting the distal tufts in L1 were stronger in looped than non-looped IT neurons for both projections (Figure 5L; V2L→V1 SRI: −0.47 ± 0.51, p=0.012; V2M→V1 SRI: −0.48 ± 0.58, p=0.022).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5L.

claim: Looped L5 neurons received a larger fraction of total FB input in their L1 apical domain compared to non-looped neurons.
source: This resulted in looped neurons receiving a larger fraction of total FB input in their L1 apical domain (mean fraction of total input in L1; V2L→V1: looped, 23.1 ± 16.6%, non-looped, 11.0 ± 10.6%, p=0.01, signed-rank test; V2M→V1: looped, 18.1 ± 23.0%, non-looped, 9.4 ± 18.2%, p=0.01, signed-rank test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: V2L- and V2M-projecting L5 populations had similar apical dendritic morphologies, with slender tufts that were indistinguishable in L1.
source: First, V2L- and V2M-projecting populations had similar apical dendritic morphologies, with slender tufts that were indistinguishable in L1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: V2L→V1 total and perisomatic inputs did not distinguish between looped L5 IT and PT neurons.
source: As with the looped vs. non-looped IT comparison, V2L→V1 total and perisomatic inputs did not distinguish between looped IT and PT neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5M–P; total SRI: −0.20 ± 0.52, p=0.195; perisomatic SRI: −0.19 ± 0.62, p=0.28), but looped neurons received stronger FB input in their L1 apical compartment (Figure 5P; SRI: −0.46 ± 0.62, p=0.026), despite having less total dendritic length in L1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5M–P, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Looped L5 IT neurons received stronger FB input in their L1 apical compartment compared to PT neurons, despite having less total dendritic length in L1.
source: As with the looped vs. non-looped IT comparison, V2L→V1 total and perisomatic inputs did not distinguish between looped IT and PT neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5M–P; total SRI: −0.20 ± 0.52, p=0.195; perisomatic SRI: −0.19 ± 0.62, p=0.28), but looped neurons received stronger FB input in their L1 apical compartment (Figure 5P; SRI: −0.46 ± 0.62, p=0.026), despite having less total dendritic length in L1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5P and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Simulations showed that the weaker sCRACM responses in distal tufts of PT neurons cannot be explained by differences in passive dendritic filtering between the two cell types.
source: Simulations showed that the weaker sCRACM responses in distal tufts of PT neurons cannot be explained by differences in passive dendritic filtering between the two cell types. In the absence of connectional selectivity, the thicker apical shafts and richer apical tuft arborization of PT neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) predict that distal FB input arriving at the soma would be larger, not smaller (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The weaker distal FB input in PT neurons was not due to different levels of hyperpolarization-activated current (Ih) between the two cell types.
source: We also confirmed that the weaker distal FB input in PT neurons was not due to different levels of hyperpolarization-activated current (Ih) between the two cell types (Harris and Shepherd, 2015), since looped IT neurons still received stronger FB input in the apical tuft when measured in the presence of Ih blockers (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4 and citation to Harris and Shepherd, 2015.

claim: The stronger sCRACM signals detected in L1 reflect synaptic selectivity for the terminal tufts of looped IT neurons.
source: Thus, the stronger sCRACM signals detected in L1 reflect synaptic selectivity for the terminal tufts of looped IT neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and simulations.

claim: The apical dendrites of L5 neurons have privileged access to FB axons when the neurons loop back to the source of those axons.
source: We conclude that the apical dendrites of L5 neurons have privileged access to FB axons when the neurons loop back to the source of those axons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: FB inputs to the basal dendrites of L5 neurons do not favor looped neurons over non-looped IT or PT neurons.
source: Conversely, FB inputs to the basal dendrites of L5 neurons do not favor looped neurons over non-looped IT or PT neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: FF input from V1 was equally strong in looped and non-looped L2/3 IT neurons in both V2L and V2M when assessing total input strength and perisomatic innervation.
source: FF input from V1 was equally strong in looped and non-looped L2/3 IT neurons in both V2L and V2M when assessing total input strength (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; V1→V2L SRI: −0.04 ± 0.30, p=0.65; V1→V2M SRI: −0.05 ± 0.35, p=0.683) and perisomatic innervation (Figure 6C; V1→V2L SRI:−0.06 ± 0.30, p=0.564; V1→V2M SRI: −0.17 ± 0.34, p=0.167).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: V1→V2M inputs in L1 were significantly stronger in non-looped L2/3 neurons projecting to V2L, while V1→V2L inputs showed no preference.
source: However, when considering FF connections in L1, V1→V2M inputs were significantly stronger in non-looped neurons projecting to V2L, while V1→V2L inputs showed no preference (Figures 6A,B,D; V1→V2L SRI: −0.03 ± 0.66, p=0.892; V1→V2M SRI: 0.68 ± 0.52, p=0.013).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 6A,B,D.

claim: Non-looped V2M L2/3 neurons received a larger fraction of total V1 FF input in L1 compared to their looped neighbors.
source: This resulted in non-looped V2M L2/3 neurons receiving a larger fraction of total V1 FF input in L1 compared to their looped neighbors (mean fraction of total input in L1; V1→V2M inputs: looped, 2.1 ± 3.7%, non-looped, 12.6 ± 13.0%, p=0.039, signed-rank test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: V2M and V2L FB inputs to L2/3 neurons were indistinguishable between looped and non-looped neurons for total input, perisomatic input, and L1 inputs.
source: Similarly, we measured the strength of V2M and V2L FB inputs to different L2/3 IT neurons in V1. Total input was indistinguishable between looped and non-looped neurons, as were perisomatic and L1 inputs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Figure 6E–H; V2L→V1, total SRI: −0.13 ± 0.51, p=0.36, perisomatic SRI: −0.13 ± 0.54, p=0.394, L1 input SRI: −0.12 ± 0.64, p=0.553; V2M→V1, total SRI: −0.04 ± 0.36, p=0.67, perisomatic SRI: 0.03 ± 0.48, p=0.826, L1 input SRI: −0.04 ± 0.66, p=0.86).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6E–H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most (3/4) FF and FB inputs did not show projection-type specificity when innervating L2/3 neurons.
source: In summary, most (3/4) FF and FB inputs did not show projection-type specificity when innervating L2/3 neurons, with the exception of V1→V2M FF inputs, which were weaker, not stronger, when contacting dendrites of looped neurons in L1, in contrast to the looped preference observed in L5 and L6.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: In seven out of eight FF/FB projections to L5 and L6, stronger inputs to looped IT neurons were found, either in the perisomatic or apical areas, or both.
source: When comparing inputs to looped and non-looped IT neurons in L5 and L6, in seven out of eight FF/FB projections we found stronger inputs to looped IT neurons, either in the perisomatic or apical areas, or both.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figure 7.

claim: None of the four FF/FB projections to L2/3 showed stronger inputs to looped IT neurons.
source: On the contrary, none of the four FF/FB projections to L2/3 showed stronger inputs to looped IT neurons, and in the only case in which input strength differed between looped and non-looped neurons, inputs were weaker in looped neurons rather than in non-looped ones.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figure 7.

claim: When comparing looped IT neurons and PT or CT neurons, in all cases CC inputs were stronger in looped IT neurons.
source: When comparing looped IT neurons and PT or CT neurons, we found that in all cases CC inputs were stronger in looped IT neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figure 7.

claim: Most FF and FB connections are selectively wired to strongly innervate looped IT neurons in L5 and L6.
source: We conclude that most FF and FB connections are selectively wired to strongly innervate looped IT neurons in L5 and L6.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: In L5, selectivity for looped neurons involved synapses on apical, but not basal, dendrites in most cases (1/3 and 3/3 of FF and FB connections tested, respectively).
source: In L5, this selectivity involved synapses on apical, but not basal, dendrites in most cases (1/3 and 3/3 of FF and FB connections tested, respectively).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Inputs to L2/3 were either equally strong in looped and non-looped IT neurons or weaker in looped ones.
source: By contrast, inputs to L2/3 were either equally strong in looped and non-looped IT neurons or weaker in looped ones.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Depolarizations evoked by photostimulation of V2M→V1 FB axons were larger in looped L6 IT neurons than in non-looped ones.
source: In the absence of current injection, a brief LED light pulse resulted in depolarizations, but not spiking activity, in the recorded cells under these illumination conditions. Depolarizations were larger in looped IT L6 neurons than in non-looped ones (Figure 8A–C; mean amplitude; looped IT, 10.2 ± 4.8 mV; non-looped IT, 4.3 ± 3.2 mV, p=0.004, signed-rank test).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8A–C.

claim: The relative difference in input strength between looped and non-looped L6 cells measured with current-clamp LED-induced responses was similar to that measured with sCRACM.
source: The relative difference in input strength between looped and non-looped cells measured with current-clamp LED-induced responses was similar to that measured with sCRACM (Figure 8C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2; current-clamp CRI: −0.38 ± 0.35; sCRACM total input SRI with AAV2/1: −0.39 ± 0.36; sCRACM total input SRI with AAV5: −0.52 ± 0.39), indicating that sCRACM reflects actual input strength in the functioning circuit.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: sCRACM reflects actual input strength in the functioning circuit.
source: The relative difference in input strength between looped and non-looped cells measured with current-clamp LED-induced responses was similar to that measured with sCRACM (Figure 8C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2; current-clamp CRI: −0.38 ± 0.35; sCRACM total input SRI with AAV2/1: −0.39 ± 0.36; sCRACM total input SRI with AAV5: −0.52 ± 0.39), indicating that sCRACM reflects actual input strength in the functioning circuit.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of current-clamp and sCRACM measurements.

claim: Photoactivation of V2M→V1 axons induced additional spiking activity over a range of current injections in L6 neurons.
source: We then asked how V2M→V1 FB combines with bottom-up input in looped and non-looped L6 IT neurons. We injected steps of positive current at the soma through the recording pipette to mimic bottom-up depolarization, and measured evoked spiking activity while photostimulating FB axons (Figure 8D–E). Photoactivation of V2M→V1 axons induced additional spiking activity over a range of current injections (Figure 8D–E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8D–E.

claim: Looped L6 neurons spiked more frequently upon FB photoactivation than their non-looped neighbors.
source: Looped neurons spiked more frequently upon FB photoactivation than their non-looped neighbors (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Stronger FB innervation of looped IT neurons in L6 can selectively modify their spiking activity when they are concurrently depolarized by other inputs.
source: Thus, stronger FB innervation of looped IT neurons in L6 can selectively modify their spiking activity when they are concurrently depolarized by other inputs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: CC axons provide inputs to all neurons regardless of their projection type.
source: Consistent with previous reports, we found that CC axons provide inputs to all neurons regardless of their projection type (DeNardo et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2015; Kinnischtzke et al., 2016; Yamawaki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous reports.

claim: Input strength was consistently different across projection classes.
source: However, input strength was consistently different across projection classes.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: When comparing looped IT neurons with neighboring subcortical-projecting PT or CT neurons, both FF and FB inputs always innervated looped IT neurons more strongly.
source: When comparing looped IT neurons with neighboring subcortical-projecting PT or CT neurons, both FF and FB inputs always innervated looped IT neurons more strongly.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The preferential wiring of FF and FB axons to IT neurons could be guided by projection-type specific molecular cues.
source: Given the distinct gene-expression profiles of IT, PT, and CT neurons (Tasic et al., 2018), the preferential wiring of FF and FB axons to IT neurons could be guided by projection-type specific molecular cues.
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citation to Tasic et al., 2018.

claim: RV-mediated trans-synaptic retrograde tracing experiments report that V1 IT neurons receive a larger proportion of their monosynaptic inputs from higher visual cortices than do V1 PT neurons.
source: These findings accord with rabies virus (RV)-mediated trans-synaptic retrograde tracing experiments reporting that V1 IT neurons receive a larger proportion of their monosynaptic inputs from higher visual cortices than do V1 PT neurons (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2015.

claim: FF inputs from V1 to frontal cortices preferentially innervate looped neurons over PT neurons.
source: They are also consistent with studies showing that FF inputs from V1 to frontal cortices preferentially innervate looped neurons over PT neurons (Zhang et al., 2016) and that looped IT neurons in L6 of somatosensory cortex receive stronger input from motor cortex than subcortically projecting neurons (Kinnischtzke et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2016.

claim: Looped IT neurons in L6 of somatosensory cortex receive stronger input from motor cortex than subcortically projecting neurons.
source: They are also consistent with studies showing that FF inputs from V1 to frontal cortices preferentially innervate looped neurons over PT neurons (Zhang et al., 2016) and that looped IT neurons in L6 of somatosensory cortex receive stronger input from motor cortex than subcortically projecting neurons (Kinnischtzke et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kinnischtzke et al., 2016.

claim: Inputs from retrosplenial cortex to primary motor cortex do not show a preference for IT over CT or PT neurons.
source: Conversely, inputs from retrosplenial cortex to primary motor cortex do not show a preference for IT over CT or PT neurons (Yamawaki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yamawaki et al., 2016.

claim: Single-cell RV tracings in V1 L6 found that CT neurons had a greater fraction of presynaptic partners from other cortical areas than IT neurons.
source: Similarly, while we found a strong preference of V2L inputs for IT over CT neurons, single-cell RV tracings in V1 L6 found that CT neurons had a greater fraction of presynaptic partners from other cortical areas than IT neurons (Vélez-Fort et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vélez-Fort et al., 2014.

claim: All the projections in this study contacted looped IT neurons.
source: All the projections in this study contacted looped IT neurons, consistent with previous reports from the visual (Johnson and Burkhalter, 1997; Kim et al., 2020), somatosensory (Kinnischtzke et al., 2016), frontal (Zhang et al., 2016), and motor (Mao et al., 2011; Yamawaki et al., 2016) cortices.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous reports.

claim: For all CC visual afferents in this study, IT neurons were the principal excitatory targets in deep layers.
source: Thus, for all CC visual afferents in this study, IT neurons were the principal excitatory targets in deep layers, and in most of these cases, looped IT neurons were the main recipients.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: In most cases, looped IT neurons were the main recipients of CC visual afferents in deep layers.
source: Thus, for all CC visual afferents in this study, IT neurons were the principal excitatory targets in deep layers, and in most of these cases, looped IT neurons were the main recipients.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The specificity of CC connections for looped neurons in infragranular layers was not absolute, as monosynaptic CC inputs were detected in all cell types.
source: The specificity of CC connections for looped neurons in infragranular layers was not absolute, as we detected monosynaptic CC inputs in all cell types.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The measurements likely underestimate the selectivity of CC inputs for looped neurons.
source: However, our measurements likely underestimate the selectivity of CC inputs for looped neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential limitations of the study.

claim: Many, if not most, projection neurons target multiple cortical areas.
source: First, many, if not most, projection neurons target multiple cortical areas (Economo et al., 2016; Han et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Economo et al., 2016 and Han et al., 2018.

claim: Some non-looped neurons might in fact send a looped projection despite not being retrogradely labeled, thereby reducing the observed specificity for looped neurons.
source: Thus, since retrograde tracer injections only label a fraction of neurons projecting to the injection site, some non-looped neurons might in fact send a looped projection despite not being retrogradely labeled, thereby reducing our observed specificity for looped neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential limitations of the study.

claim: Looped connectivity would be underestimated if it only involves CC afferents originating from a specific layer.
source: Second, looped connectivity would also be underestimated if it only involves CC afferents originating from a specific layer, as we expressed ChR2 non-specifically in projection neurons spanning multiple layers.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential limitations of the study.

claim: The absence of loop specificity in L2/3 is unlikely to be caused by looped neurons being misattributed as non-looped neurons due to incomplete labeling from tracer injections.
source: While the axons of most L2/3 neurons branch to innervate multiple cortical areas, especially those of V1 neurons projecting to V2L (Han et al., 2018), the absence of loop specificity in L2/3 is unlikely to be caused by looped neurons being misattributed as non-looped neurons due to incomplete labeling from tracer injections. This is because L5 showed looped connectivity despite having a larger percentage of neurons with bifurcating axons (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of L2/3 and L5 data, supported by citation to Han et al., 2018.

claim: A recent report using RV-mediated monosynaptic input tracing found that looped L2/3 neurons in V1 had a greater percentage of presynaptic partner cells in visual areas to which they projected.
source: A recent report using RV-mediated monosynaptic input tracing found that looped L2/3 neurons in V1 had a greater percentage of presynaptic partner cells in visual areas to which they projected (Kim et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2020.

claim: The connectivity rules of CC projections in L2/3 are different from those in deep layers, in which neurons consistently received stronger inputs from areas they innervated.
source: Thus, the connectivity rules of CC projections in L2/3 are different from those in deep layers, in which neurons consistently received stronger inputs from areas they innervated.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The selectivity of CC inputs for looped neurons might vary across individual cortical projections.
source: Alternatively, the selectivity of CC inputs for looped neurons might vary across individual cortical projections.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential variability in connectivity rules.

claim: Both FF and FB inputs innervated the perisomatic and apical dendrites of L5 IT pyramidal neurons, but they differed in their apical distribution.
source: We found that both FF and FB inputs innervated the perisomatic and apical dendrites of L5 IT pyramidal neurons, but that they differed in their apical distribution.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: FB innervated the distal dendritic tufts in L1 while FF inputs extended along the apical shaft up to L2.
source: FB innervated the distal dendritic tufts in L1 while FF inputs extended along the apical shaft up to L2 (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: For both FF and FB projections to looped L5 neurons, stronger selectivity for apical dendrites than for perisomatic ones was observed.
source: For both FF and FB projections to looped L5 neurons, we observed stronger selectivity for apical dendrites than for perisomatic ones (Figure 5, Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 7.

claim: This preference for apical dendrites was found in three out of the four CC projections studied when comparing looped with non-looped IT neurons.
source: This preference was found in three out of the four CC projections studied (including in all FB pathways) when comparing looped with non-looped IT neurons, suggesting an important role for the apical dendritic trees of L5 IT neurons in many looped hierarchical interactions.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The apical dendritic trees of L5 IT neurons may play an important role in many looped hierarchical interactions.
source: This preference was found in three out of the four CC projections studied (including in all FB pathways) when comparing looped with non-looped IT neurons, suggesting an important role for the apical dendritic trees of L5 IT neurons in many looped hierarchical interactions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Inputs to apical tufts might be selectively involved in recurrent computations, while perisomatic inputs might mediate other hierarchical exchanges.
source: Inputs to apical tufts might be selectively involved in recurrent computations, while perisomatic inputs might mediate other hierarchical exchanges.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential functional roles of different inputs.

claim: The apical arbors of L5 pyramidal neurons can perform complex computations combining inputs from different dendritic compartments through a dynamic interplay of active and passive membrane properties.
source: Through a dynamic interplay of active and passive membrane properties, the apical arbors of L5 pyramidal neurons can perform complex computations combining inputs from different dendritic compartments (Larkum, 2013; London and Häusser, 2005; Stuart and Spruston, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Larkum, 2013, London and Häusser, 2005, and Stuart and Spruston, 2015.

claim: The apical dendrites of L5 IT neurons are less well understood than those of PT neurons, being thinner and less experimentally tractable.
source: The apical dendrites of L5 IT neurons are less well understood than those of PT neurons, being thinner and less experimentally tractable.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: FF inputs to V2M were selectively stronger when contacting dendrites of non-looped L2/3 IT neurons in L1.
source: While inputs to L2/3 neurons were for the most part equally strong in looped and non-looped IT neurons, FF inputs to V2M were selectively stronger, not weaker, when contacting dendrites of non-looped IT neurons in L1 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Distal input in L2/3 neurons might be selectively involved in looped interactions, albeit with different rules than L5 neurons.
source: Thus, as with L5 neurons, distal input in L2/3 neurons might also be selectively involved in looped interactions, albeit with different rules.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential functional roles of distal inputs in L2/3.

claim: The selective engagement of looped neurons by both FF and FB afferents supports several theories advocating looped computations in CC circuitry.
source: The selective engagement of looped neurons by both FF and FB afferents supports several theories advocating looped computations in CC circuitry (Bastos et al., 2012; Guerguiev et al., 2017; Keller and Mrsic-Flogel, 2018; Mumford, 1992; Rao and Ballard, 1999; Richards and Lillicrap, 2019; Roelfsema and Holtmaat, 2018; Sacramento et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to theoretical work.

claim: L5/6 IT neurons might be preferential players in the implementation of long-range loops.
source: Our observations suggest that L5/6 IT neurons might be preferential players in the implementation of these long-range loops.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: CC inputs and postsynaptic neurons in their target area have similar tuning properties.
source: CC inputs and postsynaptic neurons in their target area have similar tuning properties (Glickfeld et al., 2013; Huh et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018) and overlapping receptive fields (Marques et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Glickfeld et al., 2013, Huh et al., 2018, Zhang et al., 2018, and Marques et al., 2018.

claim: CC inputs and postsynaptic neurons in their target area have overlapping receptive fields.
source: CC inputs and postsynaptic neurons in their target area have similar tuning properties (Glickfeld et al., 2013; Huh et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018) and overlapping receptive fields (Marques et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Marques et al., 2018.

claim: Given the prominence of looped connectivity in FF and FB visual pathways, related visual signals are likely relayed back and forth between interconnected neurons located at different hierarchical levels.
source: Thus, given the prominence of looped connectivity in FF and FB visual pathways, related visual signals are likely relayed back and forth between interconnected neurons located at different hierarchical levels.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and knowledge about tuning properties.

claim: According to recent models, looped FB innervation could allow neurons embedded in a hierarchical network to optimize synaptic weights toward the global desired output, akin to the backpropagation algorithm used to train artificial neural networks.
source: According to recent models, looped FB innervation could allow neurons embedded in a hierarchical network to optimize synaptic weights toward the global desired output, akin to the backpropagation algorithm used to train artificial neural networks (Guerguiev et al., 2017; Lillicrap et al., 2016; Richards and Lillicrap, 2019; Roelfsema and Holtmaat, 2018; Sacramento et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: The apical dendrites of looped neurons are integral to many models wherein apical inputs trigger synaptic plasticity of basal inputs to instruct learning.
source: The apical dendrites of looped neurons are integral to many such models, wherein apical inputs trigger synaptic plasticity of basal inputs to instruct learning.
evidence: This is supported by knowledge of theoretical models.

claim: Selective targeting of the apical compartments of looped neurons by descending inputs may allow L5 IT neurons to update synaptic strengths based on activity in the higher-order areas that they project to.
source: Thus, selective targeting of the apical compartments of looped neurons by descending inputs, as observed here, may allow L5 IT neurons to update synaptic strengths based on activity in the higher-order areas that they project to.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential functional implications of the findings.

claim: L5 PT neurons receive more inputs from frontal and associative areas than IT neurons.
source: Since L5 PT neurons receive more inputs from frontal and associative areas than IT neurons (Kim et al., 2015), their thicker apical dendrites might be specialized in mediating top-down processes that do not require excitatory looped connectivity, such as brain state-dependent and attentional modulations of perceptual saliency (Manita et al., 2015; Takahashi et al., 2020; Takahashi et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2015, Manita et al., 2015, Takahashi et al., 2020, Takahashi et al., 2016, and Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: The thicker apical dendrites of L5 PT neurons might be specialized in mediating top-down processes that do not require excitatory looped connectivity, such as brain state-dependent and attentional modulations of perceptual saliency.
source: Since L5 PT neurons receive more inputs from frontal and associative areas than IT neurons (Kim et al., 2015), their thicker apical dendrites might be specialized in mediating top-down processes that do not require excitatory looped connectivity, such as brain state-dependent and attentional modulations of perceptual saliency (Manita et al., 2015; Takahashi et al., 2020; Takahashi et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations.

claim: Models in which descending projections modulate plasticity in lower-order synapses to optimize the global output of the network result in alignment of FF and FB weights.
source: Models in which descending projections modulate plasticity in lower-order synapses to optimize the global output of the network result in alignment of FF and FB weights, such that synaptic strengths between pairs of reciprocally connected neurons tend to become similar (Guerguiev et al., 2017; Lillicrap et al., 2016; Sacramento et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: In the presence of weight symmetry, FF and FB projection neurons would be expected to receive minimal input from areas they do not project to, and to receive strong input from areas that they do.
source: In the presence of weight symmetry, FF and FB projection neurons would be expected to receive minimal input from areas they do not project to, and to receive strong input from areas that they do.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from theoretical models.

claim: Alignment of synaptic weights between neuron pairs will lead to stronger average synaptic input to looped neurons from both ascending and descending pathways.
